cells.tense: You are carrying what was handed to you, and you keep changing its shape so it still lands.
cells.ask: Ask one person what they'd need to hear this again, and rewrite the telling around their answer before you use it on anyone else.
cells.core:
You carry what came before you, and you don't carry it frozen. Each time you hand something over, it gets tested against the person in front of you and comes back adjusted. What arrives has your corrections already built in, which is why it still gets through.
That takes holding two things at once — what was given and what you can't yet see — and waiting past the itch to fill in the fog. Let the next step show itself and the line stays live. Small corrections, no announcement, and the current keeps running. Nothing about this needs to be declared out loud. The adjusting is the transmission, and it works because you don't stop doing it.
cells.sheetLine: You hand on what you were given, and you keep it alive by adjusting it.
cells.verb: Handing on what was learned before you, in words the next person can use
cells.place: Standing with someone in fog, where the next step shows and the rest stays hidden

cells.tense: You will keep sealing the windows so the version you hold stays the only one left standing.
cells.ask: Pick the rule you enforce hardest and run one exception to it on purpose this week, in front of the people who expect the rule.
cells.core:
A version lives in your hands, and you're spending energy keeping it correct. The letter held tight enough that the spirit has nowhere to move. When someone brings a different reading, part of you grades it before they finish the sentence, and the grading is faster than the hearing.
It shows up as a kind of bracing — you're a step ahead of the room, defending a form that only stays alive if someone keeps revising it. The fog around you isn't the problem. It's where the next version is waiting. You don't have to lower anything for good. Find out what happens when one wall goes and the roof holds, and whether what you were protecting was the form or the people.
cells.sheetLine: You enforce the version so hard the teaching can't breathe.
cells.verb: Handing on what was learned before you, in words the next person can use

cells.tense: You have been working without a shelf of what others already tried, and the not-reaching has become a habit.
cells.ask: Write down one thing you figured out alone, then ask someone older how they learned it, and keep both answers side by side for a week.
cells.core:
You build your understanding from scratch, and it holds up well enough that nobody flags the pace. No shared shelf, no ladder of what people already tried — each problem gets solved again in your own head, and that is a slower room to think in than it needs to be.
There's real intelligence in that, and real loneliness. The line that would deliver something you didn't personally discover is quiet right now. Effort isn't the gap, and neither is feeling. It's the pattern underneath the practices — how meaning travels, why a ritual holds. Look for that before you look for more material to master, and let someone else's version sit next to yours without either one having to win.
cells.sheetLine: You keep teaching yourself what someone already knew.
cells.verb: Handing on what was learned before you, in words the next person can use
cells.place: Standing with someone in fog, where the next step shows and the rest stays hidden

cells.tense: You are already the one people copy from, and you keep calling it just how you happen to talk.
cells.ask: Name one habit of yours that someone visibly picked up, tell that person you noticed it, and say out loud that it came from you.
cells.core:
People are already taking things from you. A phrase you use, the order you do things in, the way you decide when nothing is clear — it spreads, and it spreads because they watched. That is the passing-on happening. You just don't put your name on it.
You'd say you're doing your own thing. Meanwhile someone three rooms away is repeating your method. The pen is moving and no one has claimed it, which leaves what you hand over half-accidental. Nothing needs to change about what you do. One plain sentence is missing — that this started here.
The fog you move through is the fog they're learning to move through by watching you. Saying so won't make you responsible for their life. It just makes the line yours.
cells.sheetLine: You're already the source. You keep calling it nothing in particular.
cells.verb: Handing on what was learned before you, in words the next person can use
